analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate lower drug prices and use the savings to shrink seniors' prescription coverage gap.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2009 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it; it died at the end of the 111th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare drug plans leave a "coverage gap" (often called the donut hole) where seniors pay full price for prescriptions. This bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, the way the VA and other federal agencies that buy in bulk already do, and required every dollar saved in Medicare's drug account to go toward raising the coverage limit so fewer seniors fall into the gap. It arrived in the Senate with a small bipartisan group of cosponsors and was sent to the Finance Committee, which never held a vote on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare Part D who currently pay full price for prescriptions once they hit the coverage gap; their out-of-pocket costs would have been reduced as negotiated savings raised the initial coverage limit. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly, since the savings mechanism was designed so government spending did not rise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the 2003 "non-interference" rule and directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers, giving HHS authority similar to other federal agencies that buy prescriptions in bulk [S3].
Requires every dollar Medicare saves through negotiation to be used to raise the initial coverage limit under Part D, so fewer beneficiaries fall into the coverage gap, starting with 2010 [S3].
The Secretary must negotiate for each fallback drug plan and must join negotiations for any covered drug at the request of a drug plan or Medicare Advantage drug plan [S3].
The bill includes a guardrail to preserve plan competition: HHS may not impose a particular formulary or price structure on Part D plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would have earned less from Medicare Part D sales once the government could negotiate prices; possibly plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers if direct federal negotiation squeezed their margins. If negotiations saved less than expected, seniors' gap relief would be correspondingly smaller by design.

drawbacks.text: The savings mechanism is self-limiting: gap relief only grows as fast as the Medicare actuary estimates negotiation savings, so if the negotiation authority produced modest savings, seniors would see little relief [S3].
The prohibition on imposing a formulary or price structure limits how hard HHS could push manufacturers, weakening the bargaining position compared with systems abroad [S3].
Drug makers argue that lower government-negotiated prices reduce revenue available for developing new medicines, a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh.
The bill took effect on enactment but gave no transition timeline for manufacturers and plans, and the Office of the Actuary's savings estimates would drive the whole benefit with no backstop [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: seniors pay less in the coverage gap, drug makers accept lower Medicare revenue. The bill's own design hedges both ways — it forbids HHS from dictating formularies or prices (protecting plan competition) but also ties seniors' relief directly to estimated savings, so the benefit is only as large as the negotiation succeeds in being. Independent analysts at the time generally projected that direct Medicare negotiation alone would produce smaller savings than the 2003 non-interference rule's defenders and critics alike hoped or feared, and this bill never advanced far enough to generate a congressional cost estimate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled action on it, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the bill on January 15, 2009, joined at introduction by a bipartisan group including Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrats Whitehouse, Kohl, Kerry, Johnson, and Boxer [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The committee took no markup or vote during the two-year Congress, so the bill never reached the Senate floor [S1] [S5].
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill — 10 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the existing law under which the government may not negotiate Part D prices, and Medicare beneficiaries continued paying full price in the coverage gap until separate legislation addressed it in 2010.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D plans

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan but small — 10 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — and since the bill never got a vote, no record exists of how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the rule that keeps the government from negotiating Part D prices, directly cutting manufacturer revenue on drugs sold to Medicare beneficiaries. The industry's interest ran against seniors' pocketbooks, since every negotiated dollar saved was earmarked to shrink the coverage gap.

industries.industry: Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Direct federal negotiation could have squeezed the intermediaries' role in setting drug prices, though the bill barred HHS from imposing formularies or price structures, limiting the disruption. Intermediaries kept collecting premiums and administering plans regardless.
